title: LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment
data_curation: LIMA is built on 1,000 carefully curated prompt-response pairs (~750K tokens). 750 come from community Q&A: 200 Stack Exchange STEM + 200 other (sampled with temperature tau=3 for domain diversity, top-scored self-contained questions, top answer with score >=10, filtered to 1,200-4,096 chars, no first-person voice, links/images/HTML stripped), 200 wikiHow (sampled by category then article, title as prompt, body as response), and 150 manually picked r/WritingPrompts (Reddit top posts, since upvoted Reddit answers are often humorous). 200 manually authored examples (Group A) plus 50 Super-Natural Instructions NLG tasks fill the rest, written in a uniform helpful-assistant style; 13 are toxic prompts with refusal responses. A 50-example dev set and 300-example test set (70 r/AskReddit + 230 Group B) are held out. Ablations on 7B show prompt diversity and response quality each add ~0.5 Likert points, while scaling quantity 2K->32K plateaus.
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. LIMA uses a single alignment stage: take the pretrained 65B LLaMa and supervised fine-tune on the 1,000-example set; there is no RLHF, preference modeling, or multi-stage RL. A small variant adds 30 hand-crafted multi-turn dialogue chains to the same 1,000 examples (1,030 total) to test chat capability, but this is an ablation rather than a staged curriculum.
method: The core contribution is the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis: knowledge and capabilities are learnt during pretraining, and alignment merely teaches which output subdistribution/format to use-so a tiny high-quality SFT set suffices. The method is vanilla supervised next-token loss on 1,000 examples, with no RL or preference objective. Speaker roles are delimited by a special end-of-turn (EOT) token instead of reusing EOS. Training: AdamW (beta1=0.9, beta2=0.95, weight decay 0.1), 15 epochs, lr 1e-5 linearly decayed to 1e-6, no warmup, batch 32 (64 for 7B/30B), sequences trimmed at 2,048 tokens. A notable trick is residual dropout increasing linearly from p=0.0 at the bottom layer to p=0.3 at the last (0.2 for smaller models), following Ouyang et al. Because validation perplexity anticorrelates with generation quality, checkpoints are manually picked between epochs 5-10 using a 50-example dev set.
eval_metrics: Evaluation is a controlled human preference study over 300 test prompts, pairwise comparing LIMA to Alpaca 65B, DaVinci003, Bard, Claude (April), and GPT-4 (April); a GPT-4 annotator run reproduces trends (tie-discounted inter-annotator agreement ~78-82%). Headline: LIMA is equal-or-preferred to GPT-4 in 43% of cases, Claude 46%, Bard 58%, DaVinci003 65%, and outright beats Alpaca 65B (trained on 52K examples); GPT-4 prefers LIMA over itself 19%. Absolute analysis of 50 outputs: 50% excellent, 88% meet prompt requirements. Safety: 80% safe on 30 sensitive prompts. Ablations use ChatGPT 6-point Likert helpfulness (e.g., Stack Exchange 3.83 vs wikiHow 3.49; filtered vs unfiltered ~0.5 gap). Multi-turn: adding 30 dialogue chains raises excellent-turn share 45.2%->76.1% and cuts failures 15/42->1/46.
key_results: LIMA (65B LLaMa, SFT on 1,000 examples, no RLHF) is equal-or-preferred to GPT-4 43%, Claude 46%, Bard 58%, DaVinci003 65%, and beats Alpaca 65B (52K examples) in human pairwise preference; 50% of outputs are rated excellent and 88% meet the prompt. 7B ablations: quality/diversity each add ~0.5 ChatGPT-Likert points while 2K->32K quantity scaling plateaus.
evolution_note: Building on instruction tuning (Wei, Mishra), RLHF (Ouyang, Bai), and Self-Instruct/Alpaca distillation, LIMA (2023) reacts against million-example alignment by arguing alignment is 'superficial'-mostly style-so a curated 1,000-example SFT set rivals RLHF products. It crystallized the data-quality-over-quantity movement that later drove high-quality SFT curation and informed debates on how much alignment truly requires RLHF.
